<problem>
Fix an integer \(n\geq5\). Define \(\mathcal E_n\subseteq\{2,4,6,\ldots\}\) as follows. An even integer \(\beta\geq2\) belongs to \(\mathcal E_n\) if the following property holds for every choice of data \((M,g,P,f_0)\) satisfying these assumptions:

- \((M,g)\) is a smooth connected compact \(n\)-dimensional Riemannian manifold without boundary, and its scalar curvature is nonnegative everywhere.
- \(P\in M\) has a coordinate neighborhood with coordinates \(x\), centered at \(P\), in which \(g_{ij}=\delta_{ij}\).
- \(f_0\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)\), with \(f_0(P)=0\) and \(f_0<0\) on \(M\setminus\{P\}\). In the specified coordinates,
  \[
  f_0(x)=-Q_\beta(x)+O(|x|^{\beta+1}),
  \]
  where \(Q_\beta:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is a polynomial satisfying \(Q_\beta(tx)=t^\beta Q_\beta(x)\) for every \(t>0\), and \(Q_\beta(x)>0\) whenever \(x\neq0\).

The required property is that there exists \(\varepsilon>0\), allowed to depend on these data, such that for every constant \(0<\lambda<\varepsilon\), the equation
\[
-\Delta_g u=(f_0+\lambda)u^{(n+2)/(n-2)}\qquad\text{on }M
\]
has no smooth solution satisfying \(u>0\) everywhere. Here \(\Delta_g=\operatorname{div}_g\nabla_g\), so it equals \(\sum_i\partial_{x_i}^2\) in the specified flat coordinates.

Determine \(\mathcal E_n\) explicitly as a function of \(n\).
</problem>

A complete answer to this problem: A complete answer must explicitly specify the set \(\mathcal E_n\) for every integer \(n\geq5\), by a formula or an equivalent necessary-and-sufficient condition on the even integer \(\beta\) in terms of \(n\). It must decide membership for every such pair \((n,\beta)\).

One agent, working alone, was asked to find the answer, which it was not told, and to prove it, writing Python that checks every step. It may be wrong, and it may not have proved it: agents sometimes stop at bounds or partial results, and sometimes claim a proof of a wrong answer anyway. 3	Put
4	\[
5	a_n=\frac{n(n-2)}{n+2}.
6	\]
7	Then the answer is
8	\[
9	\boxed{\mathcal E_n=\{\,\beta\in2\mathbb N:\ \beta<a_n\,\}.}
10	\]
11	Equivalently,
12	\[
13	\boxed{\mathcal E_n
14	=\left\{2k:1\le k\le
15	\max\left(1,\left\lfloor\frac{n-4}{2}\right\rfloor\right)\right\}.}
16	\]
17	Thus the first few sets are
18	\[
19	\begin{array}{c|c}
20	n&\mathcal E_n\\ \hline
21	5,6,7&\{2\}\\
22	8,9&\{2,4\}\\
23	10,11&\{2,4,6\}\\
24	12,13&\{2,4,6,8\}.
25	\end{array}
26	\]
27	
28	We prove both directions. The nonexistence argument does not actually require the scalar-curvature assumption. For the other direction, our counterexamples will be flat tori, so they satisfy that assumption.
29	
30	Throughout, write
31	\[
32	p=\frac{2n}{n-2},\qquad q=p-1=\frac{n+2}{n-2},
33	\qquad h=-f_0.
34	\]
35	Thus the equation is
36	\[
37	-\Delta_g u=(\lambda-h)u^q. \tag{1}
38	\]
39	
40	## 1. Nonexistence when \(\beta<a_n\)
41	
42	Here \(h\ge0\), its only zero is \(P\), and near \(P\),
43	\[
44	h(x)=Q_\beta(x)+O(|x|^{\beta+1}).
45	\]
46	Positivity and homogeneity of \(Q_\beta\) give, in a sufficiently small coordinate ball,
47	\[
48	c|x|^\beta\le h(x)\le C|x|^\beta,
49	\qquad x\cdot\nabla h(x)\ge c h(x). \tag{2}
50	\]
51	The derivative estimate follows from the smooth Taylor expansion and
52	\(x\cdot\nabla Q_\beta=\beta Q_\beta\).
53	
54	Most importantly,
55	\[
56	H:=\int_M h^{-q}\,dV_g<\infty
57	\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
58	\beta q<n.
59	\]
60	Our hypothesis \(\beta<a_n=n/q\) therefore implies \(H<\infty\).
61	
62	Suppose \(u>0\) solves (1). Define
63	\[
64	A=\int_M h u^p\,dV_g,\qquad
65	J=\int_M h u^q\,dV_g.
66	\]
67	Integrating (1) gives
68	\[
69	J=\lambda\int_M u^q\,dV_g. \tag{3}
70	\]
71	In particular, \(J>0\).
72	
73	All constants below may depend on the fixed data, but not on \(u\) or sufficiently small \(\lambda\).
74	
75	### 1.1. Uniform estimates away from \(P\)
76	
77	On any fixed compact subset of \(M\setminus\{P\}\), for sufficiently small \(\lambda\),
78	\[
79	\Delta_g u=(h-\lambda)u^q\ge c u^q.
80	\]
81	Consequently, \(u\) is uniformly bounded on every smaller compact subset.
82	
83	For completeness, this is the elementary local Keller–Osserman estimate. In a sufficiently small geodesic ball, take
84	\[
85	W(x)=C(R^2-d(x,x_0)^2)^{-2/(q-1)}.
86	\]
87	For sufficiently large \(C\),
88	\(\Delta_g W\le cW^q\), while \(W\to\infty\) at the boundary. An interior positive maximum of \(u-W\) contradicts
89	\(\Delta_g(u-W)\ge c(u^q-W^q)>0\).
90	Local elliptic estimates then bound \(\nabla u\) away from \(P\).
91	
92	### 1.2. A first Pohozaev estimate
93	
94	Choose a fixed small Euclidean coordinate ball \(B_r\) on which (2) holds. The critical Pohozaev identity is
95	\[
96	-\frac1p\int_{B_r}(x\cdot\nabla h)u^p\,dx
97	=
98	\int_{\partial B_r}
99	\left[
100	r(\partial_\nu u)^2-\frac r2|\nabla u|^2
101	+\frac{n-2}{2}u\partial_\nu u
102	+\frac r p(\lambda-h)u^p
103	\right]d\sigma. \tag{4}
104	\]
105	Indeed, it follows by taking the divergence of
106	\[
107	(x\cdot\nabla u)\nabla u-\frac{x}{2}|\nabla u|^2
108	+\frac{n-2}{2}u\nabla u+\frac{x}{p}(\lambda-h)u^p;
109	\]
110	the undifferentiated nonlinear terms cancel because \(n/p=(n-2)/2\).
111	
112	The bounds away from \(P\) control the right side of (4). Using (2), and controlling the integral outside \(B_r\) by the same exterior bound, gives
113	\[
114	A\le C. \tag{5}
115	\]
116	
117	Weighted Hölder gives
118	\[
119	\begin{aligned}
120	\int_M u^q\,dV_g
121	&=\int_M (hu^p)^{q/p}h^{-q/p}\,dV_g\\
122	&\le A^{q/p}H^{1/p}.
123	\end{aligned} \tag{6}
124	\]
125	Together with (3) and (5), this proves
126	\[
127	J\le C\lambda. \tag{7}
128	\]
129	
130	### 1.3. Sharpening the boundary estimates
131	
132	On a fixed region away from \(P\), \(u\) is subharmonic. The local mean-value estimate for nonnegative subharmonic functions, together with \(h\ge c>0\) there, gives
133	\[
134	u\le C J^{1/q}
135	\quad\text{away from }P. \tag{8}
136	\]
137	
138	We also claim the stronger derivative estimate
139	\[
140	|\nabla u|\le CJ
141	\quad\text{on }\partial B_r. \tag{9}
142	\]
143	To prove it, let \(G\) be the normalized Green function of \(-\Delta_g\). From (3),
144	\[
145	\int_M |(\lambda-h)u^q|\,dV_g
146	\le\lambda\int_Mu^q+\int_Mhu^q=2J. \tag{10}
147	\]
148	In the Green representation for \(\nabla u(x)\), \(x\in\partial B_r\), split the integration into \(B_{r/2}\) and its complement.
149	
150	* On \(B_{r/2}\), the kernel is bounded, so (10) gives a bound \(CJ\).
151	* On the complement, (8) gives
152	  \(\lvert(\lambda-h)u^q\rvert\le CJ\). The Green-gradient estimate
153	  \[
154	  |\nabla_xG(x,y)|\le C\,d_g(x,y)^{1-n}
155	  \]
156	  has uniformly bounded integral in \(y\), again giving \(CJ\).
157	
158	This proves (9).
159	
160	Apply (8)–(9) in (4). Its boundary terms are bounded by
161	\[
162	C\left(J^2+J^{1+1/q}+J^{p/q}\right).
163	\]
164	Since \(p=q+1\), and \(1<p/q<2\), (7) allows us to assume \(J\le1\), and hence all these terms are bounded by \(CJ^{p/q}\). Outside \(B_r\), (8) gives the same bound for \(\int hu^p\). We conclude that
165	\[
166	A\le CJ^{p/q}. \tag{11}
167	\]
168	
169	Finally, (3), (6), and (11) imply
170	\[
171	J\le \lambda H^{1/p}A^{q/p}\le C\lambda J.
172	\]
173	Since \(J>0\), this is impossible when \(\lambda\) is sufficiently small.
174	
175	Therefore
176	\[
177	\boxed{\beta<a_n\implies\beta\in\mathcal E_n.} \tag{12}
178	\]
179	
180	## 2. A variational existence criterion
181	
182	We will use the following standard critical-exponent minimization argument, including its compactness proof.
183	
184	Let \(F\in C^\infty(M)\) satisfy
185	\[
186	\max_M F=L>0,\qquad \int_M F\,dV_g<0.
187	\]
188	Let \(S_n\) be the sharp Euclidean Sobolev constant:
189	\[
190	S_n=\inf_{0\ne v\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)}
191	\frac{\int_{\mathbb R^n}|\nabla v|^2}
192	{\left(\int_{\mathbb R^n}|v|^p\right)^{2/p}}.
193	\]
194	Define
195	\[
196	I_F=\inf_{\int_MF|v|^p>0}
197	\frac{\int_M|\nabla v|^2\,dV_g}
198	{\left(\int_MF|v|^p\,dV_g\right)^{2/p}}. \tag{13}
199	\]
200	
201	We claim
202	\[
203	0<I_F<S_nL^{-2/p}
204	\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
205	-\Delta_g u=Fu^q
206	\text{ has a smooth positive solution}. \tag{14}
207	\]
208	
209	Here are the details.
210	
211	Normalize a nonnegative minimizing sequence by
212	\(\int Fv_k^p=1\). It is bounded in \(H^1(M)\). Otherwise, since its gradients are bounded, its averages would tend to infinity. Dividing by those averages would give convergence to \(1\) in \(H^1\), hence in \(L^p\), contradicting \(\int F<0\).
213	
214	The same observation shows \(I_F>0\): if the energies tended to zero, a subsequence would converge in \(H^1\) to a constant, again contradicting the constraint and \(\int F<0\).
215	
216	After taking a subsequence, write
217	\[
218	v_k\rightharpoonup v\quad\text{in }H^1,\qquad
219	b=\lim_k\int_M|v_k-v|^p.
220	\]
221	The local sharp Sobolev inequality and strong \(L^2\) convergence give
222	\[
223	I_F\ge \int_M|\nabla v|^2+S_nb^{2/p}. \tag{15}
224	\]
225	Set \(D=\int_MFv^p\). The Brezis–Lieb splitting gives
226	\[
227	1-D=\lim_k\int_MF|v_k-v|^p\le Lb. \tag{16}
228	\]
229	
230	If \(D\le0\), (15)–(16) contradict \(I_F<S_nL^{-2/p}\).
231	
232	If \(0<D<1\), then
233	\[
234	\begin{aligned}
235	I_F
236	&\ge I_FD^{2/p}+S_nL^{-2/p}(1-D)^{2/p}\\
237	&>I_F\bigl(D^{2/p}+(1-D)^{2/p}\bigr)>I_F,
238	\end{aligned}
239	\]
240	another contradiction.
241	
242	If \(D\ge1\), (15) and
243	\(\int|\nabla v|^2\ge I_FD^{2/p}\) force \(D=1\) and \(b=0\).
244	Thus the infimum is attained.
245	
246	The Euler–Lagrange equation is
247	\[
248	-\Delta_g v=I_FFv^q.
249	\]
250	Critical elliptic regularity gives a bounded, then smooth, solution; one may obtain the initial higher integrability by the usual truncated-power test, absorbing the tail of
251	\(Fv^{p-2}\in L^{n/2}\).
252	The strong maximum principle gives \(v>0\). Finally,
253	\[
254	u=I_F^{1/(q-1)}v
255	\]
256	solves the required equation. This proves (14).
257	
258	## 3. Counterexamples when \(\beta>a_n\)
259	
260	Take a flat \(n\)-torus \(T^n\). Choose a smooth function \(h\) such that
261	\[
262	h(x)=|x|^\beta
263	\quad\text{near }P,\qquad
264	h>0\quad\text{on }T^n\setminus\{P\}.
265	\]
266	Such an \(h\) exists because \(\beta\) is even: \(|x|^\beta\) is a polynomial, and we can smoothly interpolate to a positive constant outside a coordinate ball.
267	
268	Set \(f_0=-h\). These data satisfy every assumption in the question, with
269	\[
270	Q_\beta(x)=(x_1^2+\cdots+x_n^2)^{\beta/2}.
271	\]
272	
273	Fix any
274	\[
275	0<\lambda<\frac1{\operatorname{Vol}(T^n)}
276	\int_{T^n}h\,dV.
277	\]
278	Then
279	\[
280	F=\lambda-h,\qquad \max F=\lambda,\qquad \int F<0.
281	\]
282	We will prove
283	\[
284	I_F<S_n\lambda^{-2/p}. \tag{17}
285	\]
286	
287	### 3.1. Bubble estimates
288	
289	Put \(s=(n-2)/2\), and take a cutoff \(\chi\), supported where \(h=|x|^\beta\), with \(\chi=1\) near \(P\). Define
290	\[
291	v_\delta(x)=\chi(x)
292	\left(\frac{\delta}{\delta^2+|x|^2}\right)^s.
293	\]
294	Let
295	\[
296	U(x)=(1+|x|^2)^{-s},\qquad
297	A_0=\int_{\mathbb R^n}U^p,\qquad
298	B_0=\int_{\mathbb R^n}U^q,
299	\]
300	and
301	\[
302	E_0=\int_{\mathbb R^n}|\nabla U|^2.
303	\]
304	The sharp Sobolev inequality, attained by \(U\), says
305	\[
306	E_0=S_nA_0^{2/p}. \tag{18}
307	\]
308	
309	Direct radial integration gives
310	\[
311	\int|\nabla v_\delta|^2=E_0+O(\delta^{n-2}), \tag{19}
312	\]
313	\[
314	\int v_\delta^p=A_0+O(\delta^n), \qquad
315	\int v_\delta^q=B_0\delta^s+O(\delta^{s+2}). \tag{20}
316	\]
317	Writing \(b=\min(\beta,n)\), it also gives
318	\[
319	\int h v_\delta^p
320	=O\!\left(\delta^b(1+|\log\delta|)\right), \tag{21}
321	\]
322	where the logarithm is needed only if \(\beta=n\).
323	
324	Since \(\beta>a_n>2\),
325	\[
326	\int h v_\delta^q=O(\delta^{s+2}),\qquad
327	\int h v_\delta^{p-2}=O(\delta^2). \tag{22}
328	\]
329	For example, the first estimate in (22) reduces to the integrability near zero of \(r^{\beta-3}\), and the second to that of \(r^{n+\beta-5}\).
330	
331	Consequently, for our fixed \(\lambda\),
332	\[
333	\int Fv_\delta^p
334	=\lambda A_0-
335	O\!\left(\delta^b(1+|\log\delta|)\right), \tag{23}
336	\]
337	and
338	\[
339	\int Fv_\delta^q
340	=\lambda B_0\delta^s+O(\delta^{s+2}). \tag{24}
341	\]
342	
343	### 3.2. Adding a small positive constant
344	
345	For \(z,t\ge0\) and \(p>2\),
346	\[
347	0\le(z+t)^p-z^p-pz^{p-1}t
348	\le C_p(z^{p-2}t^2+t^p).
349	\]
350	Apply the lower inequality to the \(\lambda\)-part of \(F\), and the upper inequality to its \(-h\)-part. Then
351	\[
352	\begin{aligned}
353	\int F(v_\delta+t)^p
354	\ge{}&\int Fv_\delta^p
355	+pt\int Fv_\delta^q\\
356	&-Ct^2\int hv_\delta^{p-2}
357	-Ct^p. \tag{25}
358	\end{aligned}
359	\]
360	
361	Choose
362	\[
363	t=\eta(\lambda\delta^s)^{1/q},
364	\]
365	where \(\eta>0\) is a sufficiently small fixed number. The main positive term in (25) is
366	\[
367	pB_0\eta(\lambda\delta^s)^{p/q},
368	\]
369	whereas \(Ct^p=C\eta^p(\lambda\delta^s)^{p/q}\). Thus the latter is absorbed by choosing \(\eta\) small.
370	
371	Now
372	\[
373	\frac{sp}{q}=\frac{n(n-2)}{n+2}=a_n.
374	\]
375	The remaining errors are of smaller order than \(\delta^{a_n}\), because
376	\[
377	b>a_n,\qquad n-2>a_n,
378	\]
379	and
380	\[
381	2+\frac{2s}{q}-a_n
382	=\frac8{n+2}>0.
383	\]
384	Using (22)–(25), for sufficiently small \(\delta\),
385	\[
386	\int F(v_\delta+t)^p
387	\ge \lambda A_0+c_\lambda\delta^{a_n},
388	\qquad c_\lambda>0. \tag{26}
389	\]
390	
391	Adding a constant does not change the energy:
392	\[
393	\int|\nabla(v_\delta+t)|^2
394	=E_0+O(\delta^{n-2}). \tag{27}
395	\]
396	Because \(a_n<n-2\), equations (18), (26), and (27) imply
397	\[
398	\frac{\int|\nabla(v_\delta+t)|^2}
399	{\left(\int F(v_\delta+t)^p\right)^{2/p}}
400	<
401	\frac{E_0}{(\lambda A_0)^{2/p}}
402	=S_n\lambda^{-2/p}
403	\]
404	for small enough \(\delta\). This is (17).
405	
406	The criterion in Section 2 now produces a smooth positive solution for every
407	\[
408	0<\lambda<\frac{\int h}{\operatorname{Vol}(T^n)}.
409	\]
410	In particular, these fixed data have positive solutions for arbitrarily small \(\lambda\). Therefore
411	\[
412	\boxed{\beta>a_n\implies\beta\notin\mathcal E_n.} \tag{28}
413	\]
414	
415	## 4. There is no even-integer borderline
416	
417	We have
418	\[
419	a_n=n-4+\frac8{n+2}.
420	\]
421	If \(a_n\) is an integer, then \(n+2\mid8\). For \(n\ge5\), the only possibility is \(n=6\), giving \(a_6=3\), which is odd.
422	
423	Thus no allowed \(\beta\) equals \(a_n\). Equations (12) and (28) settle every case.
424	
425	## 5. Executed Python checks
426	
427	The proof above is analytic; finite numerical tests cannot replace its universal arguments. The following code checks the symbolic cancellations and exponents used in it, independently evaluates the bubble integrals by quadrature, and checks the stated classification over a substantial range. I executed these checks successfully.

431	import mpmath as mp
432

434	p = 2*n/(n-2)
435	q = (n+2)/(n-2)
436	s = (n-2)/2
437	a = n*(n-2)/(n+2)
438	
439	# Symbolic identities used in both halves of the proof.
440	identities = {
441	    "p = q+1": p-q-1,
442	    "Holder threshold": n/q-a,
443	    "critical Pohozaev cancellation": n/p-(n-2)/2,
444	    "KO barrier exponent": s*q-s-2,
445	    "bubble gain exponent": s*p/q-a,
446	    "cutoff error exponent":
447	        (n-2-a)-2*(n-2)/(n+2),
448	    "mixed remainder exponent":

450	    "2 - p/q": (2-p/q)-4/(n+2),
